caption: Figure 1. Sample accounting and response-panel effects. (a) The cerebellum and hippocampus matrices contain 53 region libraries from 29 Source Name animals. (b) Points are mean gene-level log2 effects; bars are 95% percentile intervals from 1,000 animal bootstraps within label and age. All regions of a sampled animal remain together. Panel labels are inherited exploratory gene sets, not measured transcriptional time windows. Intervals are conditional on normalization and cohort exchangeability.

Figure 2. Unadjusted panel effects across 17 primary design contrasts. Numbers show mean log2 effects; an asterisk denotes BH q < 0.05 across all 232 panel tests, including metadata sensitivities. Positive effects follow the numerator in each row. Cb, cerebellum; Hip, hippocampus; HGC, habitat ground control; VGC, vivarium control. OSD-563, OSD-564 and OSD-612 are three regions of one RR-10 animal cohort, not independent missions. Glial and endothelial transcript abundance does not directly measure inflammation or barrier permeability.

Figure 3. Ground-anchor sensitivity and transfer. Dots show the observed change in squared contrast coefficients outside the Sensor31 genes after genome-expression projection or ground-calibrated score subtraction. Lines show 95% percentile ranges from 200 ground-animal bootstraps within age and cohort, conditional on normalized counts and a fixed target. These ranges describe anchor uncertainty, not complete sampling intervals or calibrated gene-level inference. The within-OSD-525 evaluation shares nine HGC animals with its anchor and is displayed as such. Negative reductions are retained. Removing expression variation is not proof of removing confounding.

Figure 4. RR-23 disjoint-anchor partitions. Each of 126 partitions trains on four of nine HGC animals plus the same eight VGC animals, then evaluates the nine FLT animals against the remaining five HGC animals. Training and evaluation animals are disjoint within a partition. Partitions reuse the same cohort and do not constitute 126 independent validations. (a) Removing sensor effect energy does not ensure a reduction outside the sensor. (b) λ is derived from conditional OLS t probabilities and is a dispersion diagnostic, not a measure of biological truth or empirical false-positive rate.

Figure 5. Count-model robustness and biological candidate sensitivity. (a) The 120 panel comparisons summarize 15 regional contrasts fitted using PyDESeq2; agreement is analytical robustness on the same observations, not independent replication. (b) Full and metadata-excluded hippocampal ISS-T flight contrasts for SRG and circadian panels. Circles are log-expression effects with 1,000-animal-bootstrap percentile intervals; hollow diamonds show mean unshrunk negative-binomial effects for the full data. q values use the complete 232-test panel family. Exclusions remove the older FLT ISS-T support; the full SRG result does not establish a region-specific mechanism.

Figure 6. Independent training–target Gaussian mechanism benchmark. Five scenarios each contain 200 independently generated datasets (1,000 datasets; 7,000 method rows including additional oracle-ground and partial-correction references in the supplement). Four operational methods are shown without target tuning. Translucent violins show the full repetition distributions where variable; points and bars are means ±1.96 Monte Carlo standard errors, not real-data confidence intervals. Biological FDP compares discoveries with the original biological coefficient vector and therefore differs from conditional statistical FDR under residual nuisance. Power and biological energy retention are undefined when no biological effects exist. Failure under overlapping biology or changed coupling is retained. The simulator is not a complete RNA-seq generative model.

Figure 7. Bounded score geometry and joint uncertainty. (a) Unbounded score gain for all 15 aligned anchor–target geometries; the bounded operator has gain at most two. (b) Observed sensor-panel effect-energy removal for matched hippocampal recovery and the RR-23 shared-HGC comparison. (c) Observed outside-sensor energy removal and 500-bootstrap percentile intervals, refitting normalization, anchor and target on each resample. Shared RR-23 HGC animals are sampled once for both roles. Intervals remain conditional on the fixed initially retained gene universe and observational sampling assumptions; zero crossings and negative reductions are shown. A point estimate may lie outside a biased percentile interval. Energy removal does not measure biological recovery.

Figure 8. Paired regional interactions. (a) Source Name matching identifies 24 RRRM-2 and 10 RR-10 cerebellum–hippocampus animal pairs. (b) All eight panel effects in primary regional contrasts; no test has q≤0.05 across the complete 104-test family, including sensitivities. (c) Individual SRG hippocampus-minus-cerebellum scores; outlined points identify metadata conflicts. (d) SRG regional flight coefficients with 2,000-animal-bootstrap percentile intervals and complete-family q values. The approximate three-way interaction uses 9,999 restricted-model wild draws. Metadata exclusion removes all older FLT ISS-T animals, reducing the sensitivity to younger-animal exposure support.

Figure 9. Exploratory high-gain stress benchmark. All 16 combinations of true gain (8 or 12), training size (24 or 96), target size (24 or 48) and unchanged or flipped outside-sensor nuisance coupling are shown. Each uses 100 independent repetitions (1,600 datasets; 6,400 method rows). Known biology is supported outside Sensor31 and is preserved exactly by both score operators. Error bars are ±1.96 Monte Carlo standard errors. Bounding reduces worst score amplification under coupling reversal but leaves substantial nuisance, including under unchanged coupling; neither norm control nor exact sensor-null preservation establishes accurate biological recovery.

Supplementary Figure 1. Conservative regional gene reproducibility screen. A candidate must have the same effect direction in every constituent contrast and finite component Wald p values; its intersection–union p value is the maximum component p. Discordant or unavailable effects receive p=1. All 54,989 region–gene combinations enter one global BH and BY family. No gene survives either correction. Component comparisons come from the same negative-binomial fits and can share samples; concordant direction alone is not replication evidence. Ranked nominal candidates are explicitly exploratory.
